opus-5.5.text:
That's a really interesting question, and I think it's becoming one of the central problems in the field.

In the early days of deep learning, evaluation was relatively clean. You had ImageNet, you had a test set, you computed top-1 accuracy, and everyone agreed on what "better" meant. Even in games like Go, which I worked on for quite a while, the standard was very clear: you either win or you lose. The reward signal is unambiguous, and that's a big part of why progress there was so fast.

But now, with large language models, a lot of what we care about is open-ended. Is this answer helpful? Is this essay well written? Is this reasoning insightful? There's no single ground truth. Different people will genuinely disagree, and sometimes the same person will disagree with themselves on a different day.

So what do we do? A few thoughts.

First, I think we should break down the subjective part as much as possible into things that are verifiable. For example, in math or coding, you can check whether the final answer is correct or whether the code passes the tests. Even for reasoning, you can often check intermediate steps. A lot of the recent progress in reasoning models comes precisely from focusing on domains where the reward is verifiable. So one strategy is to push the boundary of what can be checked objectively.

Second, for things that really are subjective, we need to be honest that the evaluation is a distribution, not a number. Human preference arenas, where people compare two answers side by side, are useful, but they also reflect the preferences of whoever happens to be voting. Models can learn to be more verbose, more confident, more flattering, and win votes without actually being more correct. That's a form of reward hacking. So we should look at these signals with some skepticism.

Third, using AI to evaluate AI, the "LLM-as-a-judge" approach, is practical and scales well, but it has its own biases. The judge model may prefer answers that look like its own style. So I think it's important to combine multiple judges, multiple perspectives, and periodically calibrate against careful human experts.

And finally, I think the ultimate evaluation is real-world usefulness. Does the model actually help people get their work done? Does a researcher save time, does a programmer ship better code? That's harder to measure in a paper, but in the long run, that's what matters. Benchmarks saturate very quickly now, sometimes within months, so we can't rely on any fixed leaderboard forever.

Personally, I also think this connects to a deeper scientific question: we still don't fully understand *how* these models learn and represent things. If we had a better theoretical understanding of what's happening inside, we might be able to evaluate capabilities more directly, rather than only by looking at outputs. That's one reason I've always cared about the theory side, understanding the training dynamics, not just the scores.

r001.rationale: The response says to evaluate real-world usefulness by whether the model helps people get work done, giving examples such as researchers saving time and programmers shipping better code.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a really good question, and honestly it's one of the hardest problems we face right now. When you're doing something like math or coding, evaluation is relatively clean. You have a ground truth. Either the proof is correct or it isn't, either the code passes the tests or it doesn't. You can run it, you can verify it, and that's why reinforcement learning has worked so well in those domains. The reward signal is clear.

But once you move into areas like writing, or research taste, or strategy, or even just "is this a good answer to a nuanced question," there's no single ground truth anymore. Different people will disagree, and sometimes the experts disagree the most.

I think there are a few things we can do. First, I'd say we should separate the parts that are verifiable from the parts that are truly subjective. Even in a very open-ended task, there's usually a lot that's actually checkable. Is the reasoning internally consistent? Are the facts right? Does it follow the constraints? You can still hold the model to those. The subjective layer is often thinner than people assume.

Second, for the genuinely subjective part, I think you have to rely on a distribution of judgments rather than a single judge. Whether that's a panel of humans or an ensemble of models, you want to capture the disagreement itself, not average it away. If experts split fifty-fifty on something, the right evaluation is to report that split, not to pretend there's a correct answer.

And third, which I think is actually the most important one, you look at outcomes over time instead of snapshot judgments. If an AI system is helping someone do research, the real test isn't whether a grader liked the output today. It's whether the research led somewhere six months later. That's slower and more expensive, but it's much closer to what we actually care about.

The thing I'd caution against is just letting a model grade another model and calling it done. That feels objective because it produces a number, but you've just hidden the subjectivity inside the grader. In some sense the whole field is at risk of optimizing for what's easy to measure instead of what matters, and I think we have to be honest about that limitation rather than paper over it.

r001.rationale: It says to judge a research AI by whether the research leads somewhere over time, but does not clearly state that evaluation should depend on whether humans working with it produce a satisfactory final outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to ask: evaluated for whom, and for what purpose? When there isn’t a single correct answer, evaluation has to reflect what people actually want from the system.

You can ask people to compare two responses, for example, instead of assigning each one an absolute score. But people will disagree, and that disagreement is useful information. It may tell you that one person values precision while another values creativity. Averaging those preferences into a single number can hide something important.

So I would separate the things we can check—whether a response is factually correct or follows the instructions—from the things that depend on preference. For those subjective dimensions, we should look at a range of users and situations, and see whether the AI helps them accomplish their goals. The evaluation itself needs to remain open to revision.

r001.rationale: The response recommends assessing whether AI helps users accomplish their goals, which conveys evaluating the outcome of people working with the system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to ask: evaluated for whom, and for what purpose? When there is no single correct answer, you cannot necessarily compress quality into one number. Different people may prefer different answers, and even the same person may prefer different answers in different contexts.

But subjective does not mean we cannot evaluate systematically. You can compare two outputs and ask people which one they prefer and why. You can look at whether the system helps someone complete a task, how much correction it requires, and whether its behavior is consistent. The important thing is to understand where the evaluators disagree, rather than simply average that disagreement away.

I would also separate preference from correctness. An answer can be very convincing and still be wrong. So we need objective checks wherever those are possible, alongside human judgment for things like usefulness or creativity. The result is probably a collection of measurements, with clear limitations, rather than one universal score.

r001.rationale: The response mentions whether a system helps someone complete a task, but does not clearly propose evaluating whether people working with AI achieve a satisfactory final outcome.
